chapter: Hollywood life and the musicians' union
title: Merging the black and white musicians' locals in Los Angeles
summary: Carter explains the disadvantages of segregated locals and credits Marl Young for the merger.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Okay. Now, the other thing that I wanted to ask you about -- there's much more that is related to Hollywood, and it goes back earlier, and I think that's in the early fifties, if I remember correctly, relating to the situation of the two segregated locals -- the black musicians local and the white local in Los Angeles. You came on the scene in the early 40's slowly, I suppose, you became more familiar with what was going on in the situation between the 2 unions, and you were a member of, of course, of the black local when you first had to join in Hollywood. What was the disadvantage of that segregated situation that led you and some others, I think, to become active in trying to overcome it? What was the disadvantage

Well, I think it's like any segregated situation where we're both supposedly members of the parent organization -- AFM -- American Federation of Musicians -- and in the local situations, there are two separate locals; one for white and one for black.

I think the feeling was at that time that the blacks were denied access to the good jobs and to the studios. As I said before, there were no blacks in the studios, with the exception of, of course, Lee Young, and I guess any other of us from studio to studio could even consider ourselves the token blacks at any given time, even when we were there just on one call. Usually, I was called when there were solos to be played, for which I was paid much above scale -- sometimes as much as 3 times scale, you know, which wasn't a lot of money for it, but was considerably more than I think -- $30 a session, at that time, in the very early days.
And of course, the indignity of being considered on the lower level, you know? And we thought we should get together and fight this and amalgamate the two locals and have just one union.
Who were some of the colleagues you were associated with in this movement to amalgamate?
Well, there were so many -- I wouldn't like to start naming names, because I wouldn't want to omit

any people who played important parts -- and so many people did, including many, many musicians. White musicians of good will, you know. Actually, we had petitions signed, and gee -- I think a couple of petitions I had signed, the first was signed, the first name on my petition was Alfred Newman, and gee, there were people like ... oh, there were just so many.

But I think, notably, I might mention Marl Young, who is the secretary of Local 47, now, and he is black, and he is a Chicago musician who also has a law degree. And he was the one who really worked very hard and drew up the proposals, under which we merged.

And if I am correct, I think the proposals that he drew up were so well done that they were just accepted in toto, or just as they were delivered, you know -- and Marl deserves a lot of credit. A lot of people say that Benny Carter was the one, but I feel it was Marl, and I always give the credit to him.
Well, of course, he gives a lot of credit to you.

Well, that's very nice. Probably the thing ... that I got around a little more than Marl and I made a little more records than Marl, and people knew my name better than they knew Marl Young's, but I feel that he was really the hard worker.
And do you feel that the situation

Yes, I think it's better; I think it's much better. Much better. And I think even the people who fought us in 767 --that was the black local -- to keep it black; you know, there were many blacks who didn't want the desegregation, you know?
But even they had come around to, you know, feeling that this was a good thing.
Yeah. Well, it's working very well. Working very well.
